extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, IP scholars, law students, biotechnology/pharmaceutical stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Legal analysis of 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility for natural products after the Supreme Court's Myriad decision, with attention to distinctions between information-encoding molecules (DNA) and non-information-encoding small molecules (e.g., Taxol) and suggested legal/policy paths forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature are unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial exclusion: phenomena of nature, natural products, laws of nature, and abstract ideas are not patentable subject matter under § 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts couch this holding in the idea that natural products do not constitute a new machine, manufacture, or composition of matter. Quotation: 'Patents cannot issue for the discovery of the phenomena of nature.' (Funk Bros.). This exclusion has been used to justify denials even where discovery meets novelty/statutory requirements; the doctrine aims to avoid granting monopolies over fundamental natural things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate breakdown: old product from new process vs degree v. kind
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-part appellate logic: (1) a patent may not be granted upon an old product though derived from a new source or process; and (2) purification steps are not patentable if the new product differs 'merely in degree, and not in kind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reasoning functions like 'pseudo-novelty' and 'pseudo-obviousness' and historically was applied under §101 as shorthand for §102/§103 concerns (Merck & Co. v. Olin Mathieson). Use this test to assess whether isolation/purification truly yields a product different in kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter eligibility is a §101 inquiry (not §§102/103/112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has held that relevant cases rest their holdings upon §101, not later sections; therefore the determination of eligibility is a distinct §101 question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While novelty/nonobviousness/disclosure may inform analysis, courts emphasize that eligibility under §101 is the controlling inquiry (Mayo). Examiners and litigants should not simply re-label §102/§103 rejections as §101 denials without addressing §101 principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated and purified exception to the natural product exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural product that has been isolated and purified can be patent-eligible—historic exception originating with Parke-Davis (adrenaline) and followed in many cases and USPTO guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exception was justified where the purified product had extraordinary utility over prior art and constituted a transformative result of human ingenuity. Examples: Parke-Davis (adrenaline), historical increase in patenting of isolated natural products pre-Myriad. USPTO previously allowed gene compositions 'isolated from its natural state' (Utility Examination Guidelines, 2001).

rubrics_metrics.name: Information-carrying nature of DNA affects §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that target the information encoded in DNA (i.e., that seek to monopolize information rather than a transformed composition) are unpatentable under §101 as held in Myriad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court emphasized that 'genes and the information they encode are not patent eligible under §101 simply because they have been isolated.' The deciding factor was concern that patents on DNA would monopolize a vast field of research by appropriating information, not merely chemical composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework for patent-eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Are the claims directed to a patent-ineligible concept (abstract idea, law of nature, product of nature)? Step 2: If so, do the claim elements contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the ineligible concept into a patent-eligible application?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation requires more than reciting the ineligible concept plus conventional steps or 'apply it' language. Alice applied this test to software; courts apply the same logic to natural-products claims to ask whether isolation/purification supplies the required inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing the §101 inquiry: focus on similarities vs differences
rubrics_metrics.description: How one frames comparison between claimed product and natural counterpart (emphasizing similarities or differences) can determine eligibility: Myriad focused on similarities (information content), leading to ineligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may look either to whether the claimed product is materially different from the natural product (differences approach) or to whether claim effectively appropriates what is the same (similarities/information approach). The article argues that focusing on information (similarities) drove Myriad's result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of claiming is not determinative but revealing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claim is worded as a composition of matter, a method, or otherwise is not dispositive of §101 eligibility; the form of claiming may instead reveal what the patentee actually seeks to appropriate (idea/information vs transformed matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO and courts have recognized that claim form can point to a deeper problem—claims that in substance claim information/ideas (even if drafted as compositions) are suspect—so claim drafting should emphasize transformative features and concrete, inventive aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption and the risk of monopolizing research tools
rubrics_metrics.description: A central policy concern in §101 is whether a claim would 'preempt' use of fundamental tools or knowledge and thereby impede future innovation; patents should not grant monopolies over basic scientific building blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mayo and Funk Bros. highlight this concern. Evaluate whether granting the claimed monopoly would 'tend to impede innovation more than it would tend to promote it.' Narrow claims that avoid broad preemption are preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/discovery v. invention normative concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are concerned with whether the patentee merely 'discovered' something in nature (as opposed to having invented a new thing), raising normative questions about whether discoverers should receive patent monopolies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although being a discovery does not ipso facto deny novelty (§102), historical cases and judicial rhetoric show reluctance to award patents where nature was the 'first and true inventor.' This underlies some §101 refusals and the 'pseudo-novelty' reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of composition-of-matter patents to incentivize drug R&D
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition of matter patents (versus process/use patents) are the most prized form of protection in pharmaceuticals because they provide long-term certainty necessary to justify multi-year, multi-billion-dollar investments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process claims are harder to enforce and FDA exclusivity is limited; therefore denying composition protection to isolated natural products biases R&D away from such drugs. Policy assessments of §101 should weigh this incentivization role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation/purification as a potential 'transformative' inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolation and purification that transform a minor natural constituent with little efficacy into a pharmaceutically useful composition can amount to the required 'inventive concept' under Alice/Mayo for non-information-encoding molecules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For molecules like Taxol (non-information-encoding), the purification materially changes utility and enables patenting historically; courts could treat such transformation as sufficient to survive step two of Alice, whereas DNA isolation does not transform the information content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish claims directed to information versus composition of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims primarily directed to the information encoded in a molecule (e.g., a gene sequence) are qualitatively different from claims directed to the physical composition that has been transformed by human effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims, determine whether their core is information/idea monopolization (which Myriad invalidated) or a new composition with changed properties/utility (potentially eligible). Draft claims to emphasize concrete structural/functional changes when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paths to clarify/revive isolated & purified exception: legislation or test-case litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two pragmatic approaches to secure patents for isolated/purified non-information-encoding natural products: (1) obtain explicit legislative clarification from Congress; or (2) bring a judicial test case to argue for a narrower reading of Myriad by the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation faces political obstacles but would be definitive. Litigation requires a plaintiff willing to invest in developing and litigating a test-case drug; it risks first-mover costs but may produce favorable precedent clarifying scope under Alice/Mayo and Myriad.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO post-Myriad guidance and its expansive reading
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has read Myriad as eliminating the isolated and purified exception for many natural products, prompting revised examination guidance (2014 PTO Guidance and later updates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be aware of PTO guidance, scholarly debate, and divergent practitioner views; argue claim drafting and evidence focused on transformative inventive concepts and the non-information-encoding character of the claimed molecule to counter PTO rejections.
